lead: A helical compression spring is a wire coiled into a helix. An axial load W makes the wire twist, so the spring stores energy like a torsion bar. The wire diameter d, mean coil diameter D and spring index C = D/d set the stress and stiffness. Curvature raises the stress on the inner side, so a Wahl factor corrects it. Deflection follows from strain energy. A long spring can buckle. A fast-changing load can make the coils surge at resonance. Springs appear in vehicle suspension, engine valves, clutches and punches.
prereq: You need torsion of a circular wire and strain energy from Unit 1, Foundations: Design Process and Stresses, plus the fatigue idea from Unit 2, Failure Theories and Fatigue Design; fatigue design of springs itself is in 4.6.

sections.h3: Wire in torsion, corrected by the Wahl factor

blocks.text: A helical compression spring is a wire coiled into a helix. An axial load W makes each coil twist; the wire carries torsion T = W D / 2. The wire diameter is d. The mean coil diameter D is measured from wire centre to wire centre. The spring index is C = D/d. The active coils N<sub>a</sub> are the coils that deflect; end coils only seat the spring. Pitch is the axial distance between centres of adjacent active coils. Solid length is the length when all coils touch. Free length is the unloaded length.
Small C means a tightly curved spring: high stress and difficult winding. Large C means a floppy spring that may buckle. Many designs use C = 4 to 12.

blocks.where: τ<sub>0</sub> is the uncorrected shear stress in Pa; W is axial load in N; D is mean coil diameter in m; d is wire diameter in m.

blocks.text: The inner side of a coil is more stressed than the outer side. The Wahl factor K<sub>w</sub> corrects for curvature and direct shear.

blocks.where: K<sub>w</sub> is the Wahl factor; C = D/d is the spring index.
τ is the maximum shear stress in Pa; other terms are as above.

blocks.text: The wire length is about π D N<sub>a</sub>. Torsion energy in that length gives the axial deflection. The result is:

blocks.where: δ is axial deflection in m; G is shear modulus in Pa; N<sub>a</sub> is active coils; W, D, d as above.
k is spring rate in N/m.

blocks.text: Energy stored is U = ½ W δ = ½ k δ². U is in joules when W is in N and δ in m. This energy is why a spring can absorb shock. The rate is linear only while the coils do not touch. At solid length the rate becomes very high.

Solid length L<sub>s</sub> = N<sub>t</sub> d, where N<sub>t</sub> is total coils including inactive end coils. Free length L<sub>f</sub> = L<sub>s</sub> + δ<sub>max</sub> + clearance, where clearance is the gap left between coils at maximum load. A common value is about 15% of δ<sub>max</sub>, so L<sub>f</sub> = L<sub>s</sub> + 1.15 δ<sub>max</sub>. A spring that is too long for its diameter can buckle sideways. If L<sub>f</sub>/D is large, guide the spring on a rod or inside a sleeve. Design so the spring does not reach solid height in service; otherwise stress rises sharply.

A sudden load sends a compression wave along the coils. If the exciting frequency matches the spring's natural frequency, the coils surge. Surge is resonance of the spring coils. Stress and noise rise, and a spring can fail even when static stress is safe.

blocks.where: f<sub>n</sub> is natural frequency in Hz for both ends fixed; ρ is wire density in kg/m³; other terms as above. One end free halves this value.

blocks.text: Keep the operating frequency fop and its harmonics away from fn. A common rule is fn ≥ 15 fop. Changing Na, d or D moves fn. Avoid cam lobes or valves that strike at fn. Fatigue under repeated load is separate; see 4.6.

Surge is worst when one end is fixed and the other is struck, as in a valve train. A damper or friction between coils reduces the amplitude. Two concentric springs can also change the natural frequency; their load sharing is in 4.6.

examples.question: A helical compression spring has mean coil diameter D = 50 mm, wire diameter d = 6 mm, N<sub>a</sub> = 10 active coils, G = 80 GPa, and carries W = 500 N. Find the Wahl factor, maximum shear stress, deflection and spring rate.
steps: k = W/δ = 500/0.04822 = 10370 N/m = 10.4 N/mm. Check formula k = Gd⁴/(8D³N<sub>a</sub>) gives the same.
examples.answer: K<sub>w</sub> = 1.176; τ<sub>max</sub> = 347 MPa; δ = 48.2 mm; k = 10.4 N/mm.
examples.check:
import math
D = 0.050
d = 0.006
N = 10
G = 80e9
W = 500
C = D/d
Kw = (4*C - 1)/(4*C - 4) + 0.615/C
tau = Kw * 8*W*D/(math.pi*d**3)
delta = 8*W*D**3*N/(G*d**4)
k = W/delta
print(f"Kw = {Kw:.3f}")
print(f"tau = {tau/1e6:.0f} MPa")
print(f"delta = {delta*1000:.1f} mm")
print(f"k = {k/1000:.1f} N/mm")

traps: Using the uncorrected stress 8WD/(πd³) and omitting K<sub>w</sub>; at small C the error is large.
Using outside diameter D<sub>o</sub> instead of mean coil diameter D; C and δ both become wrong.
Using total coils N<sub>t</sub> instead of active coils N<sub>a</sub> in the deflection and rate formulas; end coils do not deflect.
Mixing units: D and d in mm with G in GPa; convert to metres or use N/mm² consistently.
Treating surge as a static problem: if f<sub>op</sub> equals f<sub>n</sub> or a harmonic, stress rises even when static τ is safe.

quiz.q: Define spring index C and state a usual design range.
quiz.a: C = D/d, mean coil diameter divided by wire diameter. Many designs use C = 4 to 12.

quiz.q: Why is the Wahl factor greater than 1?
quiz.a: Curvature makes the inner fibre stress higher than the straight-wire torsion value; direct shear adds. K<sub>w</sub> accounts for both.

quiz.q: A spring has C = 10 and K<sub>w</sub> = 1.14. The uncorrected shear stress is 200 MPa. Find the corrected maximum shear stress.
A spring of rate 20 N/mm is compressed 15 mm. Find the force and stored energy.
A valve spring has f<sub>n</sub> = 90 Hz. The cam excites at 30 Hz with a strong third harmonic. Explain the risk.
quiz.a: The third harmonic is 30 × 3 = 90 Hz, equal to f<sub>n</sub>. Resonant surge occurs; stress and noise rise, and fatigue or failure can follow.

quiz.q: Why use active coils N<sub>a</sub>, not total coils N<sub>t</sub>, in the deflection formula?
quiz.a: End coils do not deflect; they only seat the spring. N<sub>a</sub> is the flexible part that stores energy.

quiz.q: At fixed W and d, a designer increases D. What happens to C, K<sub>w</sub>, δ and f<sub>n</sub>?
quiz.a: C rises; K<sub>w</sub> falls; the maximum shear stress rises, roughly in proportion to D (τ<sub>0</sub> ∝ D, and K<sub>w</sub> falls only slowly); δ rises as D³; f<sub>n</sub> falls as 1/D². The spring becomes softer, more surge-prone and more highly stressed.

beyond: Not for the exam. Automotive suspension and engine valve springs are designed with these formulas plus shot peening and finite element checks. Spring makers optimize wire diameter, coil count and material to cut mass while keeping surge away from engine order. Newer work uses non-circular wire, composite springs and active suspension. Search: spring surge, Wahl factor, spring optimization, shot peening residual stress.
